title: The Carrot That Used to Be Purple
blurb: Carrots were purple and yellow for centuries, and the orange part we eat is really the plant's hidden lunchbox for a spring it never gets to see.

blocks.prompt: A Whole Summer of Sunshine
blocks.text: A carrot starts as a seed. The seed is smaller than a grain of rice. You put it in soft dirt and wait. First a tiny green leaf pokes up. The leaves drink in the sunlight and make sugar. The plant sends that sugar down and packs it into its root. Day after day the root gets fatter and sweeter. That fat sweet root is the carrot. When you pull it up, you are pulling up a whole summer of sunshine. Carrots grow best in loose sandy dirt. If the root bumps into a rock, it splits and grows two funny legs.

blocks.prompt: The Carrot Was Not Always Orange
blocks.text: If you had pulled up a carrot a thousand years ago, it would not have been orange. It would have been purple, or yellow, or creamy white. The first carrots people grew came from Central Asia, in the land we now call Afghanistan. Farmers there liked the purple ones. Traders carried carrot seeds west into Europe and east into China. For hundreds of years, a carrot could be almost any color. Then, about four hundred years ago, Dutch farmers began growing orange carrots. Orange carrots were sweeter and less bitter than the old purple ones, and they did not turn the whole stew a murky purple. People liked them, so farmers grew more of them, and the orange carrot slowly pushed the others off the table. You will hear a story that Dutch farmers made carrots orange to honor their leader, William of Orange. It is a good story. Historians have never found proof of it. The real reason is simpler. Orange tasted better, so orange won. Purple and yellow carrots never disappeared. Some farmers kept growing them, and you can still buy them today.

meta.templateLabel: The Carrot That Used to Be Purple

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

The carrot is a taproot

blocks.prompt: Why a Carrot Bothers
blocks.text: A carrot is not trying to feed you. It is trying to feed itself. A carrot plant lives for two years. In the first year it does nothing but grow leaves and collect sunlight. The leaves turn that light into sugar, and the plant carries the sugar down into a swollen root called a taproot. It packs the root tight and then waits out the winter underground. In the second year the plant spends everything it saved. It shoots up tall, opens a wide lacy white flower, makes seeds, and dies. The carrot in your hand is a lunchbox the plant packed for a spring it never got to see, because we dug it up first. The orange comes from beta carotene, a pigment the plant makes while it is collecting light. When you eat it, your body breaks the beta carotene apart and builds vitamin A out of the pieces. Your eyes need vitamin A. The back of your eye uses it to make a light catching molecule inside the cells that let you see in dim rooms. People who get almost no vitamin A can go night blind. So carrots really do help your eyes, but only up to a point. Once your body has the vitamin A it needs, extra carrots do not give you better vision. They just give you extra beta carotene, and if you eat a truly enormous number, your skin can turn faintly orange. That is harmless, and it fades.

blocks.prompt: The Carrot Went to War
blocks.text: In 1940, British night fighters started shooting down German bombers in the dark with a success that surprised everyone. The reason was radar. Britain had built a secret network of ground stations and had begun fitting compact radar sets into the aircraft themselves, and it very much wanted to keep that quiet. What the public heard instead was carrots. Newspapers ran stories about a pilot named John Cunningham, nicknamed Cat's Eyes, who was said to see in the dark because he ate so many carrots. The Ministry of Food leaned in hard. It printed posters, invented a cheerful cartoon character called Doctor Carrot, and pushed carrot recipes on a hungry country: carrot jam, carrot pudding, even a carrot on a stick sold as a treat for children. Historians still argue about how much of this was aimed at fooling Germany and how much was ordinary wartime thrift. Britain had a carrot surplus and a shortage of almost everything else, so telling people to eat carrots was useful whether or not any German believed it. Either way, the story stuck. Eighty years later, children who have never heard of radar still get told that carrots help you see in the dark. There is a grain of truth underneath the propaganda. Carrots are rich in beta carotene, which your body converts into vitamin A, and vitamin A is essential to the light sensing cells at the back of your eye. Someone starved of vitamin A really does lose their night vision, and carrots really will fix that. But a well fed pilot who eats a second helping of carrots does not gain a superpower. He gains a second helping of carrots. The carrot has been quietly reinvented before. In 1986, a California farmer named Mike Yurosek was throwing away huge quantities of carrots that were bent, split, or simply the wrong shape for a supermarket shelf. He fed some of them through an industrial green bean cutter, which chopped them into short pieces, then ran the pieces through a potato peeler until they came out smooth and round ended. He had invented the baby carrot. It was not a baby anything. It was a full grown carrot that had been rescued from the bin and given a new shape, and it changed how much of the crop got eaten rather than dumped.

6.title: The Carrot That Used to Be Purple
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Carrot That Used to Be Purple

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Daucus carota, the wild carrot
Queen Anne's lace is the same species
Domesticated in Central Asia about a thousand years ago
Orange appears in Dutch records in the 1600s
One beta carotene molecule splits into two of vitamin A
The carrot genome was sequenced in 2016

blocks.prompt: The Carrot Is an Invention
blocks.text: Walk along a roadside in summer and you may pass the carrot's wild ancestor without noticing it. Queen Anne's lace, Daucus carota, stands waist high with a flat white flower like a doily. Pull one up. The root is a pale, forked, woody string, bitter enough to make you spit, and about the thickness of a pencil. Nothing about it says food. That plant and the carrot in your refrigerator are the same species. The difference is a thousand years of people choosing. Somewhere in Central Asia, around the tenth century, farmers began saving seed from the wild carrots whose roots were fattest and least bitter, planting those, and repeating. Each generation the average root got a little thicker and a little sweeter, because the thin bitter ones were not invited to reproduce. Carrot seeds traveled the trade routes west into the Middle East and Europe and east into China, and the early cultivated carrots were purple and yellow, not orange. Orange carrots emerge in Dutch records in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, apparently selected out of yellow stock, and they spread because they were sweeter, milder, and did not bleed purple into the pot. The popular tale that Dutch growers bred them orange to honor William of Orange is repeated everywhere and supported by nothing. It is a story about a story. What people were unknowingly selecting for is worth understanding. The carrot is biennial. In its first season the plant does one job: grow leaves, capture light, and pump the resulting sugar down into a taproot for storage. That store exists to fund a second season of flowering and seed. Every gardener who chose the fattest root was choosing the plant that hoarded the hardest, and hoarding is exactly what makes a carrot worth eating. We are eating a savings account. We are also eating the plant's future, which is why carrot farmers who want seed must leave some plants in the ground for a second year and let them bolt. The orange itself was a bonus nobody was aiming at. It comes from beta carotene, a pigment involved in the plant's light gathering, and it happens that the human body can cleave a beta carotene molecule and build vitamin A from the halves. Vitamin A becomes retinal, the light sensitive part of rhodopsin, the molecule in your eye that can respond to a single particle of light in a dark room. Farmers selecting for sweetness accidentally selected for a compound that maintains human night vision. That is luck, not design. None of this is unusual. Corn began as a grass with a few hard kernels. Cabbage, broccoli, kale, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts are all one species, wild cabbage, pushed in five directions by five sets of preferences. Wild almonds were bitter and poisonous. The peach was small, sour, and mostly stone. Every one of them was reshaped by people who had no idea what a gene was and who simply kept the seeds of whatever they liked best. Their work is invisible now because we call the results vegetables and assume they were always here. The carrot is not a natural object that we happened to find. It is a technology, built slowly, by hand, in the dark, by people whose names are gone.
